specStatements.text: (HT only) Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.

(HT only) When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current with the same frequency as the radio wave itself, so radio waves can themselves induce oscillations in an electrical circuit.
Changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range. Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.

Ultraviolet waves, X-rays and gamma rays can have hazardous effects on human body tissue. The effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose. Radiation dose (in sieverts) is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation.
Students will not be required to recall the unit of radiation dose.
Students should be able to draw conclusions from given data about the risks and consequences of exposure to radiation.
Ultraviolet waves can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

scopeNotes.statement: Students will not be required to recall the unit of radiation dose.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item in this section asks a student to produce the name or the symbol of the unit of radiation dose from memory, and no option is correct only because it names that unit. Wherever a dose appears — in a concept, in a misconception, or in a question stem — the unit is supplied to the student as part of the given information, and the relationship 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv) is printed in the stem of every question that requires it. The unit is used, converted and interpreted, which the specification does require through statement S05 and through drawing conclusions from given data, but it is never itself the thing being recalled.

concepts.definition: A repeated back-and-forth change in the current in a circuit, so that charge flows first one way and then the other, over and over again. The number of complete back-and-forth cycles each second is the frequency of the oscillation.

(HT only) Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. A circuit made to oscillate at a chosen frequency drives charge back and forth in a transmitting aerial, and radio waves of that frequency are sent out.

(HT only) When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current in a circuit — a current that repeatedly reverses direction rather than flowing steadily one way. In this sense radio waves can themselves induce oscillations in an electrical circuit.

(HT only) The alternating current created when a radio wave is absorbed has the same frequency as the radio wave itself. A 200 MHz wave absorbed by a receiving aerial sets up an alternating current of 200 MHz in the circuit joined to it.
Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom. They are the part of the electromagnetic spectrum whose source is nuclear rather than a change involving the electrons of the atom.

Changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range. The same kinds of change work in both directions: an atom able to emit a wave of a given frequency can also absorb one.

Radiation with enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms, leaving charged particles behind. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation, and this is why they can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

Radiation dose (in sieverts) is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation. It is not a count of waves or of decays: it is a measure of risk, and the harm depends on the type of radiation as well as on the size of the dose.

The two sizes of unit used for radiation dose in this specification are related by 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). To change a dose in mSv into Sv, divide by 1000; to change a dose in Sv into mSv, multiply by 1000.
Ultraviolet waves can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer. These are the two effects of ultraviolet on human body tissue named by the specification.

A change to a gene inside a cell. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer, so damage from these waves is damage to the material inside cells rather than simple heating of tissue.

To draw a conclusion about risk from a table of doses, first put every dose into the same unit using 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, then compare the numbers. Only once the units match does a larger number mean a larger risk of harm.

misconceptions.question: Where do gamma rays come from?
misconceptions.correct: Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.
misconceptions.misconception: Gamma rays are emitted by the electrons of an atom, in the same way that visible light is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet electron energy changes as the source of light long before they meet gamma rays, so they extend the picture they already hold to every high-energy wave. Diagrams of atoms also draw the eye to the electrons rather than to the nucleus.
misconceptions.correction: Changes in atoms and in their nuclei can both produce electromagnetic waves over a wide frequency range, but the specification names the nucleus specifically as the origin of gamma rays.

misconceptions.question: Which parts of the electromagnetic spectrum can be produced by changes in atoms?
misconceptions.correct: Changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can generate or absorb electromagnetic waves over a wide frequency range.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the nucleus can produce electromagnetic waves, so every wave in the spectrum has a nuclear origin.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Having learned the memorable fact that gamma rays come from the nucleus, students over-apply it and treat the nucleus as the source of all radiation.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in waves over a wide frequency range. The nucleus is singled out only for gamma rays.

misconceptions.question: How are radio waves produced?
misconceptions.correct: (HT only) Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.
misconceptions.misconception: Radio waves are produced by heating something until it emits, in the way a hot object emits infrared.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Emission by hot objects is the only production mechanism many students have met, so it is transferred to the radio part of the spectrum, where the real mechanism is an oscillating circuit.
misconceptions.correction: For radio waves the specification names one production mechanism: oscillations in electrical circuits.

misconceptions.question: What kind of current does an absorbed radio wave create in a circuit?
misconceptions.correct: It may create an alternating current in the circuit.
misconceptions.misconception: An absorbed radio wave creates a steady direct current, because absorbing energy should give a steady output.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'a current is produced' with cells and steady flow, and the idea of a current that reverses millions of times a second is unfamiliar.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that absorbed radio waves may create an alternating current, which is exactly why they can induce oscillations in a circuit.

misconceptions.question: What is the frequency of the current created when a radio wave is absorbed?
misconceptions.correct: It has the same frequency as the radio wave itself.
misconceptions.misconception: The induced current has a different frequency from the wave — commonly half of it, or double it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect a conversion between wave and current to change the number, by analogy with gears, transformers or the doubling they see in wave diagrams.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: the alternating current created has the same frequency as the radio wave itself.

misconceptions.question: What does a radiation dose in sieverts measure?
misconceptions.correct: It is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: A dose in sieverts counts how many radioactive atoms decayed, or how much radioactive material entered the body.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'dose' is met first in medicine, where it means an amount of a substance, so students read it as an amount rather than as a measure of risk.
misconceptions.correction: Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure, not a count of decays and not a mass of material.

misconceptions.question: A dose is 75 mSv. What is it in sieverts?
misconceptions.misconception: The number is left unchanged, so 75 mSv is written as 75 Sv.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Under time pressure students copy the number across and change only the unit, especially when the prefix milli is unfamiliar in a new context.
misconceptions.correction: 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so a dose in mSv must be divided by 1000 to give a dose in sieverts.

misconceptions.question: How many millisieverts are there in one sievert?
misconceptions.misconception: When converting mSv to Sv the student divides by the wrong power of ten — by 100 (giving 0.75 Sv) or by 10 (giving 7.5 Sv) — rather than by 1000.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The prefix milli is confused with centi, and 100 is the conversion students use most often elsewhere, for example between metres and centimetres or in percentages.
misconceptions.correction: Milli means one thousandth. The specification gives the relationship directly: 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv).

misconceptions.question: What decides how much harm an exposure to radiation does?
misconceptions.correct: The effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the size of the dose matters; the type of radiation makes no difference to the harm done.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A single number in sieverts looks like the whole story, so students treat dose as the only variable and ignore the type of radiation named alongside it.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose — both of them, not one.

misconceptions.question: What can ultraviolet waves do to the human body?
misconceptions.correct: Ultraviolet waves can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultraviolet only ages the skin, by heating it; the risk of cancer comes from X-rays and gamma rays alone.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sunburn feels like heat, so students explain ultraviolet damage as heating, and they reserve cancer for the radiations they have been told are ionising.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names two effects of ultraviolet on the body: skin ageing prematurely and an increased risk of skin cancer.

misconceptions.question: Which of ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are described as ionising radiation?
misconceptions.correct: X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultraviolet is ionising radiation, so it causes harm by mutating genes in the same way X-rays do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All three are grouped together as hazardous in the same sentence of the specification, so students merge them and give ultraviolet the mechanism named for the other two.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names X-rays and gamma rays as the ionising radiations that mutate genes; for ultraviolet it names premature ageing of the skin and an increased risk of skin cancer.

misconceptions.question: A table lists doses of 6 mSv, 18 mSv and 0.5 Sv. Which is the largest?
misconceptions.correct: 0.5 Sv is the largest, because 0.5 Sv is 500 mSv.
misconceptions.misconception: 18 mSv is the largest, because 18 is the biggest number printed in the table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students compare the digits in a table without first checking that the units in the column are the same, and 0.5 looks small next to 18.
misconceptions.correction: Convert everything to one unit first, using 1000 mSv = 1 Sv. Then 0.5 Sv becomes 500 mSv, far larger than 18 mSv.

misconceptions.question: Which electromagnetic waves can have hazardous effects on human body tissue?
misconceptions.correct: Ultraviolet waves, X-rays and gamma rays can have hazardous effects on human body tissue.
misconceptions.misconception: Hazard is judged by how frightening the source sounds, so microwaves, or radiation from far away, are ranked as the most dangerous.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday warnings about microwave ovens and mobile phones, and dramatic accounts of radiation from space, make students rank danger by familiarity or by how exotic the source is rather than by the specification's two factors.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names ultraviolet waves, X-rays and gamma rays as the ones that can have hazardous effects, and says the effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.

misconceptions.question: A worker receives a radiation dose of a few millisieverts. Is there any risk of harm?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, a small risk. Radiation dose in sieverts is a measure of the risk of harm, and the risk grows as the dose grows — it does not switch off at small doses.
misconceptions.misconception: Small radiation doses are completely safe, so all workers on small-sounding doses face the same zero risk.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday limits such as speed limits and alcohol guidelines suggest a threshold below which nothing matters, so students treat every dose that sounds small as equally harmless instead of comparing the doses.
misconceptions.correction: Dose in sieverts measures the risk of harm: the larger the dose, the larger the risk. Doses must be compared in the same unit — 0.5 Sv is 500 mSv, far larger than 6 mSv or 18 mSv, so that worker is at the greatest risk.

misconceptions.question: What harm can X-rays and gamma rays do to the human body?
misconceptions.correct: They are ionising radiation: absorbed in body tissue they can cause genes to mutate, which can lead to cancer.
misconceptions.misconception: X-rays and gamma rays act on the skin like strong sunlight, being absorbed at the surface and making the skin age early.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Premature ageing of skin is taught as a hazard of ultraviolet, and sunlight damage is the most familiar radiation harm, so students transfer this surface skin effect to every high-energy electromagnetic wave.
misconceptions.correction: Premature skin ageing is a hazard of ultraviolet. X-rays and gamma rays penetrate deep into body tissue; because they are ionising they can mutate genes and cause cancer, not surface ageing.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) How can radio waves be produced?

options.text: By oscillations in an electrical circuit
options.rationale: The specification states that radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.

options.text: By heating a metal aerial till it glows
options.rationale: Chosen by students whose only model of emission is a hot object radiating, which they transfer to radio waves.

options.text: By changes in the nucleus of the atom
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have generalised the nuclear origin of gamma rays to the whole spectrum.

options.text: By changes in the electrons of an atom
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat electron energy changes as the source of every electromagnetic wave.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) A radio wave is absorbed by an aerial joined to a circuit. What may the wave create in that circuit?

options.text: A steady direct current, always one way
options.rationale: Chosen by students who associate any produced current with the steady flow from a cell.

options.text: An alternating current in that circuit
options.rationale: The specification states that absorbed radio waves may create an alternating current, so they induce oscillations in the circuit.

options.text: A magnetic field but no current in it
options.rationale: Plausible to students who remember that a wave carries a magnetic part and stop there, missing the induced current.

options.text: A current whose frequency is doubled
options.rationale: Chosen by students who expect the frequency to change when the wave is turned into a current.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) A transmitter sends out radio waves at 200 MHz. A receiving aerial absorbs them and an alternating current is created in the circuit joined to it. What is the frequency of that current?

options.text: 100 MHz, half the frequency of the wave
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume some halving occurs when a wave is turned into a current.

options.text: 400 MHz, twice the frequency of the wave
options.rationale: The mirror-image error: students expect a doubling, by analogy with wave diagrams.

options.text: 200 MHz, the same as that radio wave
options.rationale: The specification states that the alternating current created has the same frequency as the radio wave itself.

options.text: 0 Hz, because the current is direct
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think an absorbed wave gives a steady direct current, which has no frequency.

options.text: In changes to the electrons of an atom
options.rationale: Chosen by students who use the electron model of light emission for every high-energy wave.

options.text: In bonds being broken between two atoms
options.rationale: Attractive to students who associate high energy with chemical change rather than with the nucleus.

options.text: In the heating of very dense material
options.rationale: Chosen by students who explain all emission as something hot giving out radiation.

options.text: In changes in the nucleus of an atom
options.rationale: The specification states that gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about how electromagnetic waves are generated and absorbed is correct?

options.text: Only changes in the nuclei of atoms can generate these waves
options.rationale: Chosen by students who over-apply the nuclear origin of gamma rays to the whole spectrum.

options.text: Changes in atoms and in their nuclei generate and absorb them
options.rationale: The specification states that changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range.

options.text: Only changes in the electrons of an atom can generate them
options.rationale: Chosen by students whose only model of emission involves electrons, leaving the nucleus out.

options.text: Atoms generate these waves but can never absorb any of them
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat emission and absorption as separate processes, missing 'generated or absorbed'.

mcqs.stem: A worker's radiation dose is recorded in sieverts (Sv). What does this dose measure?

options.text: The number of nuclei decaying near the worker
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read 'dose' as a count of decays rather than as a measure of risk.

options.text: The amount of radioactive material in the body
options.rationale: Chosen by students who carry the medical meaning of 'dose' as an amount of substance into physics.

options.text: The risk of harm that results from the exposure
options.rationale: The specification states that radiation dose (in sieverts) is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation.

options.text: The frequency of the radiation entering the body
options.rationale: Plausible to students who expect any radiation measurement to describe the wave itself rather than its effect.

mcqs.stem: Ultraviolet waves, X-rays and gamma rays can have hazardous effects on human body tissue. What do those effects depend on?

options.text: The size of the dose received, whatever type it is
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat the single number in sieverts as the whole story.

options.text: Only the total size of the dose, not its type
options.rationale: A student believing only dose size matters and radiation type is irrelevant selects size alone.

options.text: The distance the radiation travelled to the body
options.rationale: Chosen by students who rank hazard by everyday intuitions about nearness rather than by the two named factors.

options.text: The type of radiation and the size of the dose
options.rationale: The specification states that the effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.

mcqs.stem: A patient receives a radiation dose of 75 mSv from a scan. Use 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). What is this dose in sieverts?

options.rationale: 75 divided by 1000 gives 0.075 Sv, using the relationship 1000 mSv = 1 Sv as given in the stem.
The result of dividing by 100 instead of 1000, from confusing milli with centi.

options.text: 7.5 Sv
options.rationale: The result of dividing by 10, a common slip when the size of the prefix is not secure.

options.text: 75 Sv
options.rationale: The number is copied across and only the unit changed, so no conversion is carried out at all.

mcqs.stem: The table shows the average dose a person in the UK receives each year: radon gas 1.3 mSv, medical X-rays 0.4 mSv, cosmic rays 0.3 mSv. Which conclusion is supported by these data?

options.text: Medical X-rays give the largest yearly dose of the three
options.rationale: Chosen by students who pick the source that feels most dangerous instead of reading the numbers given.

options.text: The three sources together give a dose of over one sievert
options.rationale: The total is 2.0 mSv, which is 0.002 Sv; this option comes from mishandling the mSv to Sv conversion.

options.text: Radon gives a larger yearly dose than the other two added
options.rationale: 1.3 mSv is greater than 0.4 mSv + 0.3 mSv = 0.7 mSv, so this conclusion does follow from the data given.

options.text: Cosmic rays carry the greatest risk as they come from space
options.rationale: Chosen by students who judge risk by how exotic a source sounds rather than by the size of the dose given.

mcqs.stem: Three workers received yearly doses of 6 mSv, 18 mSv and 0.5 Sv. Use 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). Which worker is at the greatest risk of harm?

options.text: The worker on 18 mSv, the largest number shown
options.rationale: Chosen by students who compare the digits without first making the units the same.

options.text: The worker on 6 mSv, since small doses build up most
options.rationale: Plausible to students who recall that repeated small exposures matter, and use that in place of comparing the doses.

options.text: All three equally, since 6, 18 and 0.5 are small
options.rationale: A size-only student who does not convert 0.5 Sv sees three small figures and judges the risks equal.

options.text: The worker on 0.5 Sv, because that equals 500 mSv
options.rationale: Converting with 1000 mSv = 1 Sv gives 500 mSv, far greater than 18 mSv or 6 mSv, so this dose carries the greatest risk.

mcqs.stem: What effects can ultraviolet waves have on human body tissue?

options.text: Skin ages early and the risk of skin cancer rises
options.rationale: The specification states that ultraviolet waves can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer.

options.text: Genes mutate, as ultraviolet is ionising radiation
options.rationale: Chosen by students who give ultraviolet the mechanism the specification names for X-rays and gamma rays.

options.text: Skin ages early but the risk of cancer is unchanged
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember the ageing but reserve cancer for X-rays and gamma rays alone.

options.text: Skin ages early because the tissue gets heated
options.rationale: Chosen by students who explain sunburn as heating, since that is what it feels like.

mcqs.stem: Why can X-rays and gamma rays cause cancer in human body tissue?

options.text: They are absorbed by the skin and make it age early
options.rationale: Chosen by students who swap over the effects named for ultraviolet and for the ionising radiations.

options.text: They are ionising and can cause genes to mutate
options.rationale: The specification states that X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

options.text: They heat body cells until those cells are killed
options.rationale: Chosen by students whose only model of radiation damage is heating, as with infrared.

options.text: They are ionising, so they burn the skin surface
options.rationale: Half-remembered: the word ionising is kept but paired with burning rather than with the mutation of genes.
